articles.text: Monsieur Jules Grevy has been re-elected President of France after a most exciting election.
articles.summary: Brief note that Jules Grevy has been re-elected President of France.

articles.text: The Grand Junction News has issued a Year Book that is a credit to its editor and ought to do much toward building up the country, the News so ably represents.
articles.summary: Praise for the Grand Junction News's Year Book.

articles.text: There is scarcely a newspaper received at the Cow Boy office that does not ridicule the so-called state of Dakota. All over the United States the project is so laughed at that it bids fair to be jeered to death, even if it were not sure to die on its own merits or rather, lack of merit.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy says newspapers nationwide ridicule the 'so-called state of Dakota' movement.

articles.text: The rumored buying out of the Northern Pacific express Co. by the Wells-Fargo proves to be false. Word has now been received that there will be a reduction in rates after Jan 1. This may or may not be the precursor of another slashing of rates such as we had last winter, but it looks wonderfully like it.
articles.summary: Rumored Wells-Fargo buyout of the Northern Pacific express company proves false; express rates to drop after January 1.

articles.text: Last nights' papers show that the government is waking up to the fact that the Apaches in Arizona must be crushed into submission. There are only about 200 Apaches and Gen. Crook has been chasing them for a long time with 3,000 or 4,000 men. Six companies of infantry and one of cavalry in addition have been ordered for duty against the Apaches and with these the government hopes to succeed. If 200 Texas and Arizona cowboys were well armed and equipped and sent against the Apaches the Indian war would not last two months.
articles.summary: Editorial on the Apache campaign in Arizona, claiming 200 armed cowboys could end it in two months.

articles.text: The Indians are still giving great trouble in Arizona and murders by them are frequent. To a man up a tree it looks as though Congress had better stop quarrelling over the silver bill awhile and exterminate these red devils, if it takes every soldier in the United States army. To send a few companies of tenderfoot swaddies against the Indians on their chosen fighting ground is on a par with the idiocy which has all along characterized the government's treatment of the Indians. The Apaches, who are causing the present disturbances, are as barren of anything productive of sentiment as a possum's tail is of hair and it would be impossible for even Dawes' ultra-philanthropic constituents to find anything to love in them. They are the scum de la scum of the Indian nations in all that relates to deceit, treachery and blood-thirstiness and will only be improved mentally, morally or physically by being filled full enough of holes to let out their miserable lives. If necessary, let the government send 50,000 men against them and stop this shedding of innocent blood. Lives are worth more than money. Peace in the United States is more valuable than discussion as to whether we shall have greenbacks or silver dollars.
articles.summary: Violent anti-Apache editorial urging Congress to drop the silver debate and send overwhelming force against the Apaches in Arizona.

articles.text:
News came in yesterday afternoon that a Mr. Church, associated with Ben. Mason in the mercantile business, was shot and instantly killed Thursday night by some one of a number of cowboys who were enjoying themselves at Mason's bar. The shooting is said to be entirely accidental and all express deep sorrow at the occurrence. Church was said to be a favorite among the cowboys generally and a good man. The particulars of the unfortunate affair are meagre but it seems that Church was just entering the door when some one who was on the inside thoughtlessly or accidentally fired a pistol shot through the door and struck Church in the breast.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.

The above is the brief description of what is no better than a cold-blooded murder. We do not know any of the parties to the affair nor any particulars further than the above. We only know that one or more men were carrying six-shooters and that he or they had been drinking. The particular one who fired the fatal shot did not know, as the fact proves, that his shot would prove harmless. According to law, this is manslaughter in the second degree. According to the highest justice, a man who wears a revolver and then gets drunk, knowing that while under the influence of liquor he is liable to discharge it, and finally winds up by accidentally(?) shooting anyone, is no better than any other murderer. To know that at any time he may kill some one, and to still continue the drunken shooting, is equivalent to premeditation, which constitutes the distinction between murder and manslaughter. It is time that cow papers and cowmen everywhere should combine and crush out the worse than idiocy that so many times culminates fatally. A revolver in the hands of a drunken man is something altogether too dangerous to jest about. Whether it is owing to the efforts of the Cow Boy or not in this direction, the fact is certain that not one-quarter of the revolvers are now carried here, that there were two years ago. The consequence is that promiscuous shooting and the consequent accidents have decreased by more than three-fourths. We hope soon to see the time when everyone carrying a revolver will be compelled to lay it off while in town.
articles.summary: Reprinted Stockgrowers' Journal report of Mr. Church's accidental shooting at Ben. Mason's bar, with Packard's editorial calling drunken revolver-carrying murder and noting fewer revolvers now carried in Medora.

articles.text: The billiard championship of the world has been decided. Schæfer took first prize, Vignaux second and Slosson third.

articles.text:
The Express advises southern Texas stockmen to abandon the trail, as they will be compelled to do it eventually and the sooner the better. The Express should not lose sight of the fact that to abandon the drive involves a revolution in our system of handling cattle, and which new departure cannot be brought about in a day or year, but must come gradually; the drive then, must be abandoned by degrees. That no time should be lost perfecting arrangements for maturing and transporting our beef, we not only admit, but emphasize. But meanwhile, a great many of our cattle owners have young cattle, for the maturing and fattening of which they have made no provision and they need the money for the cattle. Therefore, just at present, there is no question of such vital and immediate importance to southern Texas cattlemen as that of the spring drive to the northwest.—[Texas Stockman.

The above is the frankest article in relation to the Texas trail, that we have ever seen in a Texas paper. If the whole controversy had been carried on in the same open spirit that actuated the writer of the above, there would have been none of the ill-feeling that now exists between northern and southern cowmen. It was the bull-dozing, you-will-and-you-won't style of argument that has caused the most of the trouble. The cattle business of the past made the interests of the north and south dependent on each other. In the future, except for the competition they offer, they will soon be almost as separated as if the interests were in different countries.
articles.summary: Reprinted Texas Stockman piece on the Texas trail drive, with Cow Boy comment on north-south cowmen's ill-feeling.

articles.summary: Tommy Smith is in Deadwood looking for work.

articles.summary: A daughter was born to Mr. and Mrs. Coleman on Monday.

articles.text: J. R. Grymes returned last Sunday night from his long eastern trip.
articles.summary: J. R. Grymes returned Sunday night from a long trip east.

articles.text: Johnny Munro came in from Mingusville yesterday. He will invest in stock in the spring.
articles.summary: Johnny Munro came in from Mingusville and plans to invest in stock in the spring.

articles.text: It's too bad a grind on Maxwell, so we won't say anything about his getting buck ague.
articles.summary: Joke about Maxwell getting 'buck ague'.

articles.text: Miss Finger of South Heart, attended the Christmas hop, and is now a guest of Mrs. E. G. Paddock.
articles.summary: Miss Finger of South Heart attended the Christmas hop and is staying with Mrs. E. G. Paddock.

articles.text: C. F. Ellison and wife will begin housekeeping to-day. Their home is the neatest one in Medora.
articles.summary: C. F. Ellison and his wife begin housekeeping today in what the paper calls Medora's neatest home.

articles.text: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck, came in Tuesday night and spent yesterday rustling among our cigar and liquor men.
articles.summary: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck arrived Tuesday night and canvassed Medora's cigar and liquor dealers.

articles.text: W. H. Fortier has resumed his old position as agent at Gladstone. He recently bought another farm in that vicinity.
articles.summary: W. H. Fortier is again agent at Gladstone and has bought another farm there.

articles.text: A. Osborne was in yesterday from the Ætna ranch and is as much pleased with the condition of his cattle as are the men on the river.
articles.summary: A. Osborne came in from the Ætna ranch, pleased with his cattle's condition.

articles.text: "Chicago Al" returned last week from a trip nearly to Miles City, on a successful hunt after some strayed horses of Howard Eaton's.
articles.summary: 'Chicago Al' returned from a successful trip nearly to Miles City hunting Howard Eaton's strayed horses.

articles.text: Valley City had a game of base-ball Saturday. There have scarcely been ten days this fall and winter that one could not have been played here.
articles.summary: Valley City played baseball Saturday; the Cow Boy notes Medora's mild fall and winter.

articles.text: The stag party at the HT horse ranch on Christmas day, is still the topic of conversation up the river. All the participants report a glorious time.
articles.summary: A Christmas-day stag party at the HT horse ranch is still talked about up the river.

articles.text: The Christmas tree at Mrs. Jorgens was enjoyed as much by the old people as by the youngsters. We hope there will be many repetitions of the good time.
articles.summary: Mrs. Jorgens's Christmas tree was enjoyed by old and young.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts will probably start east next month to contract cattle for spring delivery. He reports that he can lay cattle down here as cheap or cheaper than he did last year.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts plans to go east next month to contract cattle for spring delivery.

articles.text: The social hop given by Mr. and Mrs. Arch. Boyd at the Northern Pacific, was thoroughly enjoyed by all of the large number in attendance. Christmas evening could not have been spent in a pleasanter way.
articles.summary: Mr. and Mrs. Arch. Boyd gave a well-attended social hop at the Northern Pacific on Christmas evening.

articles.text: Harry Tarbell has measured some of the distances up the river with an odometer and from Medora, they are as follows: To Ferris & Merrifield's, 7½ miles; to Dantz', 15 miles; to the Logging Camp, 29½ miles; to the HT horse camp, 37½ miles. These distances will be authority in the future.
articles.summary: Harry Tarbell measured odometer distances up the river from Medora, including 7½ miles to Ferris & Merrifield's.

articles.text: J. N. Maxwell and wife intend leaving for St. Paul in two or three days. Mr. Maxwell has accepted a position as messenger for Wells-Fargo with a run between St. Paul and Fargo. He has only accepted the position for three months and will return in the spring and put in cattle. Mr. and Mrs. Maxwell are general favorites here and even a brief absence is regretted by all.
articles.summary: J. N. Maxwell and wife leave for St. Paul; he takes a three-month Wells-Fargo messenger job and will return in spring to put in cattle.

articles.text: A year ago to-day the thermometer registered forty-four degrees below zero. This morning at ten o'clock, it was thirty two above, and the light snow which fell last night had already begun to melt from the roofs. New Year's day a year ago was the coldest day of the winter, the mercury crawling down into the bulb and trying to pull the tube in after it, while spirit thermometers registered from forty-six to fifty below. Unless there is a sudden and unexpected change in the temperature, we expect to make our New Year's calls to-morrow in a linen duster and straw hat.
articles.summary: Mild weather: 32 above this morning versus 44 below a year ago; light snow last night melting.

articles.text: Never before have cattlemen in this section felt so jubilant at this time of the year. We have had no real winter weather and there has not been a day since the round-up that cattle have not been taking on fat. A ride over the ranges shows sleek, well-contented cattle that will easily stand the two months at most of winter that we can have. In all the coolies and broken country, there is an abundance of the very best feed, at present entirely untouched, but which will be of use if we have any weather that will force the cattle back from the more open ravines into the sheltered nooks. The loss so far has been nothing as the cattle thrive far better in this weather than they do in summer and the grass also is more fattening.
articles.summary: Cattlemen jubilant: no real winter yet, cattle fat and no losses, abundant untouched feed in the coulees.
